name: Japan
summary: Larry finished his service in Japan as a medical-evacuation patient. By his account (August 2026 call), he was flown out of Vietnam seriously ill — likely hepatitis, plus malaria and infections — arriving, as he remembers it, in early September 1965, with the weather turning cold into winter. His DD-214 independently confirms the Japan chapter: his last duty assignment was a U.S. Army medical command at APO SF 96343 (Camp Zama) under U.S. Army Japan. From the hospital he befriended the patient in the bed across from him, a man from back east whose name he no longer remembers; together they explored Tokyo, finding a basement German restaurant called "Heidelberg" off the Ginza. Japan is also where he remembers seeing the Stars and Stripes item reporting him killed in action. In a Tell a Story comment (2026-08-13) he named the hospital himself: "I was at Camp Zama in Japan in Sugami Uro" [read as Sagami-Ōno].
researchNotes: Larry has now named the hospital unprompted (2026-08-13 comment): told only that research had a high-confidence candidate — not which one — he wrote "Camp Zama ... in Sugami Uro" [Sagami-Ōno], converging exactly with the documentary case below. The hospital was almost certainly the U.S. Army Medical Center, Japan at Sagami-Ōno / Camp Zama — in Sept–Nov 1965 effectively the only Army hospital in Japan receiving Vietnam evacuees (the 249th General at Camp Drake and the 106th General at Kishine both opened December 1965, after he was home), and documented as admitting 462 Vietnam malaria patients in Aug–Dec 1965; APO 96343 is Camp Zama's. Full research note: research/places/japan-hospital-1965.md. Sagami-Ōno is ~40 minutes from Tokyo on the Odakyū line, an easy day trip to the Ginza for a convalescent. Remaining goals: confirm via NPRC clinical records (filed by hospital name — see research/records-request/); locate the original Stars and Stripes item and ask whether he saw it in the hospital ward; identify the German restaurant of the Ginza day (working leads and next archives in research/places/ginza-heidelberg.md); identify the hospital friend (a fellow patient from back east). Captain "Guegler" may be associated with this period. Coordinates wait on Larry confirming the hospital. 2026-08-23 (giscus-stories-c18118868): Larry puts the hospital stay at "close to 4 months" and describes the route — "Flew first to the Philippines and spent 4 days at a navy base or navy hospital. Then flown to camp Zama in Japan." The Philippines stop is new and is a documentary node in its own right (Clark AB or a Navy facility, ~4 days, early September 1965), worth naming on the NPRC clinical-records request alongside Camp Zama. Four months from an early-September arrival runs to about the end of December — later than the 30 November 1965 separation on the DD-214, so the duration is a soft estimate.
